title: Doorbell Alerts You Can See and Feel: Flashing and Vibrating Options for Hearing Loss
subtitle: A plain-English guide to strobe lights, lamp flashers and vibrating pagers that tell you someone is at the door, sometimes without replacing the doorbell you already have.
excerpt: If the doorbell rings and nobody hears it, a flashing light or a gentle buzz may help. Here is how these add-ons work, what they cannot do, and what to check before you buy.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: A missed doorbell can mean a missed package, a neighbor who gives up and walks away, or a family member left waiting on the step. For many people with hearing loss, the problem is simply that the chime is too quiet, too far away, or drowned out by the TV.

A doorbell alert turns the ring into something you can see, like a flashing light, or something you can feel, like a vibration from a pager you carry. Most of the kits described here plug into a wall outlet and need no wiring.
The UK hearing loss charity RNID notes that "a standard doorbell may not be loud enough" for some people, which is why these add-ons exist.

A vibrating pager system, as RNID describes it, has a transmitter at the door and a receiver that you carry. Flashing-light systems work along similar lines, with a receiver that lights up instead. The parts talk to each other wirelessly.

According to RNID, receivers can offer adjustable vibration, a flashing light, distinct patterns for different alerts, and placement under a pillow for night use. North Dakota Services for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing adds that a simpler pager can get your attention with a short vibration.

RNID also says an alert system can work by listening to your existing chime, so you may not need to replace the doorbell. That can matter for renters and for people in buildings with shared entry systems, who may not be able to replace the doorbell. Renters may also need a landlord's permission for any wiring, although most of these kits plug in and need none.

Some receivers handle more than the doorbell. The Bellman Visit Flash Receiver, for example, picks up doorbell, phone, smoke and baby-cry signals. UCSF EARS, a university hearing program, suggests using more than one path to get an alert, such as light, vibration and phone. It also recommends visual or vibrating alerts as the default setup for people with significant hearing loss.

items: Match the parts. Some receivers only work with certain transmitters. The Bellman receiver below works with Bellman Visit transmitters, and the Safeguard kit is listed as compatible with SS-series transmitters. Check the listing before you buy.
Decide between light and vibration. A strobe or lamp flash gives a visual signal. A pager you carry gives a physical one. Choose based on your level of hearing loss, not the product name.
Check power. Plug-in receivers need an outlet. Rechargeable receivers need to be kept charged. Alerts only work if the receiver is on and within range.
Think about nighttime. UCSF EARS recommends strobes and bed shakers as the main nighttime alert. Look for a receiver that can connect to a bed shaker.
Look at fees. None of the products below list a monthly fee in our notes, but confirm that on the seller's page.
Treat range claims with caution. Walls can block wireless signals, and a seller's stated range has not necessarily been verified.
Check the price and the return terms on the seller's page, since prices vary widely in this category.

sections.content: Setting It Up and Using It Well

Once the kit is in place, check that the receiver is switched on, charged if it runs on a battery, and within range of where you spend your time. Because walls can block the wireless signal, notice whether the alert still reaches you in the rooms you use most.
If you use a pager, give it a regular spot so it stays charged and close at hand. Where a receiver has selectable channels, as the Sonic Alert DB100 does, follow the maker's instructions to set it.
Mild hearing loss may not need any of this. If you are unsure which kind of alert suits you, an audiologist can test your hearing and advise you.

A doorbell flasher is not a fire alarm. It does not replace a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm for sleeping. UCSF EARS recommends strobes and bed shakers for fire and CO alarms at night, which is a separate purchase. Alerts also work only if the receiver is on, in range and, for battery models, charged.
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: A flashing light or a buzz from a pager is a modest gadget, but it can take some of the guesswork out of the front door. Take it one step at a time and check that the parts match before you buy.

products.name: Sonic Alert DB100 Wireless Doorbell Signaler/Transmitter
products.blurb: A wireless transmitter with a built-in chime, 64 selectable channels and an outlet that can flash a lamp. A MaxiAids listing says it works with Sonic Alert receivers, so check that the receiver you buy matches.

products.name: Flashing Strobe Wireless Chime Kit
products.blurb: A kit with a push button, a plug-in chime and a strobe with 15 flashes. It plugs into a standard 110V outlet and is listed as compatible with SS-series transmitters.

products.name: Bellman Visit Flash Receiver
products.blurb: Works with Bellman Visit transmitters and receives doorbell, phone, smoke and baby-cry signals, with four colored lights showing the source. It runs on AC or a rechargeable battery and can connect to a bed shaker.
